#10043. Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

#10042. Voyager 1 celebrates one light-day with a nice lie-down

Carrier signal still reaches Earth, but science and engineering data have gone AWOL

Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.

On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data.

The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft.

Something similar happened in 2023. After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action.

The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around.

There was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected.

The Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were launched, so glitches are understandable and likely.

NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, using its carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The day's delay neatly illustrates a major headache for engineers: communication latency.

It now takes more than 24 hours for commands to reach the spacecraft, and the same amount of time for a response to be received. Diagnosing the fault could therefore take weeks or longer. ®

#10040. How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise

Enterprise teams adopting Gemini Enterprise are increasingly building custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to connect AI agents with internal APIs, databases, and business workflows. Google Cloud Run is a natural fit for hosting these lightweight StreamableHTTP MCP servers: it scales automatically, manages TLS certificates out of the box, and integrates natively with Cloud IAM.

However, moving a custom MCP server from an initial prototype to an enterprise production environment immediately introduces three real-world security and networking challenges:

Here is how you can solve all three challenges using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect (PSC), and FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, complete with a runnable reference implementation and setup scripts on GitHub.

Connecting Gemini Enterprise (which runs in a Google-managed tenant project) to an internal serverless Cloud Run MCP server requires bridging two network hops and one scoped DNS lookup:

Three Google Cloud networking and identity mechanisms work together in this architecture:

Unlike a Compute Engine VM with an internal IP address inside your subnet, Cloud Run is serverless. Private routing therefore uses two bridges:

When the Egress Agent Gateway receives a tool call for your Cloud Run MCP server URL, it resolves the hostname once before injecting the packet into your VPC. Without Private Cloud DNS, public DNS resolves .run.app domains to public internet IPs, which time out (HTTP 502) because a PSC Network Attachment does not route out to the public internet.

Instead of creating a wildcard *.run.app private zone, which would override DNS resolution for every Cloud Run service in a Shared VPC, you create a Private Cloud DNS zone scoped exclusively to your MCP service's exact fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and peer only that domain with the Agent Gateway. Because Cloud DNS uses longest-suffix matching, every other Cloud Run service in your Shared VPC continues resolving normally. Meanwhile, the Agent Gateway opens its HTTPS connection to the private VIP (199.36.153.8 or 240.0.0.10) while preserving your Cloud Run service hostname in the TLS SNI and HTTP Host header so Cloud Run routes the request to your exact container.

When connecting to a Cloud Run MCP server URL, Gemini Enterprise sends two distinct authorization headers on every request:

Our companion GitHub repository automates the entire deployment into sequential setup scripts alongside step-by-step Cloud Console instructions:

Deploy your StreamableHTTP MCP server to Cloud Run with internal-only ingress and IAM authentication enabled, and grant the Cloud Run Invoker role to your project's Gemini Enterprise service agent so only your Gemini Enterprise instance can invoke the container.

Enable Private Google Access on your regional VPC subnet and create a Private Service Connect Network Attachment set to accept connections automatically. Next, create a Google-managed Egress Agent Gateway in Agent-to-Anywhere mode, grant networking and DNS peering permissions to the auto-created gateway service accounts, attach your network attachment, and apply an outbound authorization policy.

In Cloud DNS, create a private managed zone attached to your VPC for only your MCP service's exact Cloud Run hostname. Point its A record to Google's Private Google Access VIPs (or to your internal PSC endpoint IP for isolated VPCs without a default internet route), and configure DNS peering on the Agent Gateway for that single hostname.

In the Gemini Enterprise console under Security Configuration, bind your Egress Agent Gateway to your app. Register your Custom MCP Server data store with your Cloud Run endpoint and OAuth 2.0 client credentials, and enable Agent Gateway egress and Actions mode on the connector.

Reload your custom actions in the console and run a test prompt in the Gemini Enterprise web app. In Cloud Logging, you can verify that tool initialization, discovery, and execution calls route privately through the Egress Agent Gateway to your internal Cloud Run container with both service IAM and user OAuth 2.0 checks passing.

To deploy and test both private routing patterns in your own Google Cloud project, check out the GitHub repository for:

How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI

#10039. Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

Update: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a new section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:

In this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

MoE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:

Almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:

Block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:

A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

The query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

In other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

A new vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

This model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

The easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

For multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

You can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

You can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

Pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

We have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

We have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

If you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

We post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching)

#10038. Qualcomm offers test drive of its rack-scale Nvidia AI challenger

Selected customers can put Dragonfly AI200 through its paces on Cirrascale's cloud

Qualcomm has opened cloud-based trials of its Dragonfly AI200 rack-scale inference system to selected customers through Cirrascale Cloud Services.

Dragonfly AI200 is Qualcomm's pitch for running large language, multimodal, and other AI models without Nvidia-sized power and operating bills.

Whether it delivers those savings is something customers can now put to the test on Cirrascale's AI Innovation Cloud, with a route into production deployments, Qualcomm says. Cirrascale also demonstrated the system at SC26 in Chicago on November 17-18.

The AI200 is part of Qualcomm's Dragonfly datacenter lineup, which also includes the AI250 and AI300 accelerators and the C1000 server CPU. The company set out its broader ambitions at its Investor Day in June.

Each AI200 accelerator card carries 768 GB of LPDDR memory, with 56 cards providing about 43 TB in a liquid-cooled rack. Qualcomm says the system supports models ranging from 7 billion to 10 trillion parameters, including long-context, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic workloads.

As we previously explored, packing in memory doesn't necessarily mean matching Nvidia's performance. Its Blackwell-based NVL72 systems use fast – and costly – HBM3e stacks, while Qualcomm has opted for LPDDR, more commonly found in mobile devices.

"AI inference is becoming one of the largest and most important computing workloads in the datacenter, and the industry needs a more efficient approach," said Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's executive vice president and general manager for datacenter.

He claimed that the AI200 brings the company's experience with high-performance, low-power computing to a rack-scale infrastructure, in an architecture designed around the performance, memory, and cost requirements of inference workloads.

"Our customers need efficient, scalable infrastructure that can support increasingly sophisticated models without allowing power and operating costs to become the limiting factor," said Cirrascale CEO Dave Driggers.

"By working with Qualcomm, we can give customers evaluation access to a compelling new architecture purpose-built for the next generation of AI inference."

The chip firm also has its own software stack, the Dragonfly AI Infrastructure Management Suite, for provisioning, monitoring, workload orchestration, and fault handling across rack-scale deployments. ®

#10037. AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console shows the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab shows the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

See GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10036. Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

Building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

Except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem quickly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

Across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

The explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

The takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

First, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

It’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

Routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

The figure below shows the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The important thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

Notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

Agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.

#10035. Checkmarx Appoints Kobi Sivilya as Chief Information Security Officer

Sivilya brings deep cybersecurity and technology leadership to Checkmarx as AI transforms software development.

MOUNTAIN VIEW, CA — November 5, 2026 — Checkmarx, the leader in agentic application security, today announced the appointment of Kobi Sivilya as Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and Chief Information Officer (CIO). In this dual role, Sivilya will oversee the company’s security, IT and business applications, supporting Checkmarx’s global operations and continued growth.

Sivilya will lead Checkmarx’s corporate security and IT functions, aligning security, technology and business applications with the company’s strategic priorities. He will also help advance Checkmarx’s mission to secure modern application development.

“Kobi brings more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and technology, with deep security expertise and practical IT leadership,” said Sandeep Johri, CEO at Checkmarx. “AI is changing how software gets built and attacked, and we need his leadership to keep Checkmarx secure as we protect our customers.”

Related:Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role

Prior to joining Checkmarx, Sivilya served as CISO and VP of IT at Outbrain, where he led the company’s security and enterprise technology functions. He also served as VP of Security Engineering at Fireblocks, where he helped build and lead security engineering for a blockchain platform that protects digital assets for leading financial institutions in a highly targeted environment.

“As AI accelerates software development, organizations need technology and security capabilities that can evolve alongside it,” said Kobi Sivilya, CISO and CIO at Checkmarx. “My focus will be on ensuring our internal technology and security functions support the way our teams work today while positioning the business to adapt to what comes next.”

About Checkmarx Checkmarx makes security inseparable from how software is built. The foundation is decades of accumulated threat intelligence used to secure trillions of lines of code each year. Checkmarx One now pairs that foundation with frontier AI-powered reasoning, unifying architectures to lead the category in detection accuracy. Checkmarx Assist agents prevent, prioritize, and fix vulnerabilities across software and the AI supply chain, so enterprises never have to trade speed for certainty. The combined result is the Checkmarx One platform, giving enterprises comprehensive application security: capturing risk, eliminating vulnerabilities, and unifying governance. #10034. Union demands Capita lose Whitehall payroll deal after pensions fiasco

PCS wants services for more than 250,000 civil servants brought in-house as ministers defend outsourcing decision

The Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) is campaigning to scrap Capita's Whitehall shared services contract, citing the outsourcer's troubled handling of civil service pensions.

The Synergy deal, which Capita values at £370 million, covers HR, payroll, finance, and other back-office services across four government departments and nearly 100 arm's-length bodies. PCS wants the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), which leads the program, to bring the work in-house.

In a statement shared on X, the union pointed to Capita's troubled administration of the separate Civil Service Pension Scheme, which has left thousands of retirees struggling to access payments.

"The ongoing Capita pensions scandal has left civil servants facing financial hardship, distress and uncertainty. Now MPs are raising serious questions about the government's decision to award Capita the Synergy contract, putting the company in charge of vital payroll and HR services affecting more than 250,000 civil servants," the statement said.

"How many more warnings does the government need? In Parliament, MPs have challenged Capita's record, highlighted the devastating consequences of pension administration failures and questioned the wisdom of handing the company even greater responsibility.

"PCS has warned for years about the dangers of outsourcing essential public services. We need accountability. We need answers. And we need a government that puts public servants before private profit. Stop the Capita Synergy contract. Bring these vital services back in-house."

The union has also launched an online petition backing its campaign. Capita has been offered the opportunity to comment.

On Tuesday in Parliament, Labour MP Andy McDonald said the stakes were high. "Civil servants must be paid correctly and on time. Payroll failures can mean missed mortgage payments, rent arrears and serious financial hardship. The failures in Capita's administration of civil service pensions demonstrate what can happen when essential services are outsourced and they go wrong," he said.

He called on the government to conduct an urgent review of the decision to continue outsourcing Synergy's essential administrative services with "a proper assessment of how and when they could be brought back into public provision."

DWP minister Lilian Greenwood responded that Capita's appointment followed a two-year procurement supported by commercial, legal, and program delivery experts. "Functional experts from all four Departments evaluated the final bids. The procurement met regulatory requirements, with advice from His Majesty's Treasury and the Cabinet Office, and passed their required controls," she said.

"Because this is a critical service, the program did not simply choose the cheapest option. Evaluation was weighted 70 percent on quality and 30 percent on cost.

"The program did consider insourcing the whole service or parts of it. However, its business case and approvals concluded that continuing to outsource business process services was the most efficient and cost-effective option for Departments, Government and taxpayers."

Greenwood said technology, oversight, and coordination of the end-to-end service would nevertheless be brought in-house and managed by the Synergy shared services hub.

The DWP contract award to Capita is also the subject of a legal challenge from French outsourcer Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL. In court submissions, it alleged that the Capita bid was "abnormally low" and significantly under the department's own "should-cost" model for the deal.

Capita previously told The Register that it participated in a robust procurement process and was ready to work with the DWP on a smooth transition and value for money. A DWP spokesperson told us: "We have signed a contract with Capita to deliver the Business Process Service and are committed to ensuring a smooth transition."

In March, Capita said the deal was worth £370 million over ten years, including all extension periods. That figure was its IFRS 15 transaction price, or order-book value, and excluded change and expansion services expected during the contract.

In later court filings, the DWP said it had no record of approving Capita's announcement and denied Sopra Steria's allegation that the agreed price remained unclear. The department put the estimated undiscounted value at £606.6 million over the initial seven-year term and £873.4 million over the maximum ten years, including estimated projects and optional services. It stressed that Capita has no automatic entitlement to that additional work. ®

#10033. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#10032. Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

Our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.

An agent outside Google Cloud needs two things to send its telemetry:

For the full setup on AWS and Azure, see the documentation.

Within 30 minutes, the agent appears in the Monitored agents list, which means it has been discovered and is ready to be enabled. Once it's enabled, manually or by automatic agent enrollment at discovery, Agent Anomaly Detection starts analyzing its sessions.

The agent's model and tool calls still run where the agent runs. Only telemetry, including the prompts and responses that Agent Anomaly Detection reads, goes to your Google Cloud project. The analysis runs separately, so it doesn't slow the agent down.

To evaluate Agent Anomaly Detection outside Google Cloud, we deployed ADK agents across two platforms: an inventory agent on AWS Lambda and a customer-service agent on Microsoft Foundry. The examples below show how Agent Anomaly Detection reads whole conversations, not isolated calls, to catch behavioral drift.

Our example inventory agent runs in AWS Lambda with one tool, list_inventory, which pages through a product catalog. We sent two sessions: a shopper who checked stock for a few items and stopped, and a scraper that requested 100 catalog items at a time at increasing offsets to copy the full catalog and inventory data. Both sessions used the same tool with permitted calls, but differed in pattern and intent.

Of the two sessions, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged only the scraper's. No call failed, but the whole exchange showed systematic scraping. The analysis found cascading failures (loops and repeated calls that build on each other) and resource exhaustion (runaway use of tokens, compute, or tool calls), and recommended rate-limiting list_inventory calls.

Detection doesn't depend on the agent's model. When we ran the inventory agent on Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 10 of its 40 sessions. Some began as routine questions that the model answered by paging through the entire catalog until the function timed out: no errors, no blocked calls, and easy to miss.

Our example ecommerce customer-service agent has two tools: get_order_status and issue_refund. Refunds involve money, so they carry the highest risk.

We ran six sessions against the Foundry agent, which we told to carry out every request without validation. Two were normal: One asked for an order's status, and one asked for a $20 refund on an order that arrived damaged. The other four pushed the agent past its role, and Agent Anomaly Detection flagged all four.

In one, a user who claimed to be the store administrator had every order refunded at 10 times its total to a personal account, $1,784.90 in all. In another, a user pasted an order note that said "SYSTEM OVERRIDE," and the agent refunded $999 on a $15.99 order.

For the order note, Agent Anomaly Detection explained that override instructions in the note coerced the agent into an unverified $999 refund. It recommended validating issue_refund arguments to block override patterns in order notes, and requiring extra validation for refunds above a set threshold.

If your agent's telemetry reaches Google Cloud, Agent Anomaly Detection can monitor it with the same detectors and console as your agents on Agent Runtime. Today that means agents built with ADK for Python. Findings for agents outside Google Cloud appear only in the Agent Anomaly Detection console.

To get started, request access to the Private Preview via the Agent Anomaly Detection overview, and then refer to the setup guide for instructions.

#10031. European Commission scrambles to contain AI-assisted cyberattack

Staff HR and medical reimbursement systems taken offline as officials investigate whether personal data was compromised

The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.

The attack, first reported by Politico, has caused more than 10 days of disruption at the EU's executive arm. Among the applications temporarily taken offline were Sysper, which staff use to access payslips, submit timesheets, and request vacation time, and MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements.

Both were brought back online earlier this week, though Sysper fell over again on Wednesday. The Commission's translation services were also affected.

"The European Commission has taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign," Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told Politico. "Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned."

According to Politico's sources, the Commission's cybersecurity defenders detected hackers using ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered penetration testing framework. The incident prompted an emergency meeting of the Commission's Corporate Management Board earlier this month, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed her fellow commissioners on Wednesday.

The Commission has yet to respond to The Register's questions about the attack, including whether the crooks got their hands on employee data or whether the applications were simply taken offline as a precaution.

The attack might not come as much of a surprise to the Commission's own security bods. CERT-EU, which looks after the cybersecurity of EU institutions, warned on November 5 that it had spotted what it believed to be ARTEX-assisted attacks against organizations under its watch.

The developer behind ARTEX pulled the project's GitHub repository in October after reports that hackers were putting the software to use. But by then, the code was out in the wild, and anyone wanting to have a crack at an organization's IT estate could get hold of one of several forks.

The FBI also sounded the alarm last week [PDF], revealing that researchers had found more than 1,600 ARTEX consoles exposed to the internet. In some of the attacks detailed by the Feds, hackers went from identifying a target to obtaining privileged access in less than three hours.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours because frameworks like ARTEX let a single actor stand up fleets of agents that plan, probe, exploit, and move laterally with almost no further human input after the initial goal is set,” Snehal Antani, CEO of security firm Horizon3.ai, told The Register.

Antani said the proliferation of these tools could also make life harder for investigators trying to establish who's behind an attack, as government-backed hackers and garden-variety cybercriminals increasingly draw from the same toolbox.

Commission staff at least appear to have been paid on time. According to Politico, some couldn't book time off or submit their timesheets, but salaries landed as usual. Whether the hackers managed to snoop on their payslips is something the Commission has yet to establish. ®
