#9988. US let Nvidia and AMD sell bucketloads of chips to military-linked Chinese companies

Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.

The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.

BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.

But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies, the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.

Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.

Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.

One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.

Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.

Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.

Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”

“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said.

But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.

Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.

Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.

And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.

That’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®

#9987. What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

Questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully."

Note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

What has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:

Participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:

51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:

35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:

The paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

An evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

We have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a new arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗

The most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:

Pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

Some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics said "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check."

So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

To the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

Stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗

It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

I have been working on a complementary experiment at https://ReproducibleAIList.org, though not the same scale. We've been taking models from Chip Huyen's GoodAIList.com and having a clean-room agent try to reproduce each one from scratch using the code repos (not the papers).

One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.

Very cool, roar sounds like a great package! I'll take a look and see what we can learn from roar

Really enjoyed being part of this experiment. Gratifying to see our reproduction highlighted as one of the community’s best.

“A Coin Flip for Safety” was reproduced using AlphaXiv’s OpenResearch with OpenCode’s free BigPickle model, with experiments run locally on 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090s.

It was a great demonstration of how agent-assisted research can make independent reproduction and auditing accessible with relatively modest compute.

That gives us bilibili the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

The scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days shows how quickly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻

What I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊

The point about reviewing capacity is particularly important... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️

Most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨

Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion.

In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.

Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine.

Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework.

I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.

This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked:

“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”

“I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.”

In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit.

GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground

With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate.

With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit.

Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all.

As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer.

The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new ACCESSIBILITY.md file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the ACCESSIBILITY.md file.

Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked:

“How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?”

#9985. Big Tech's compliance with EU market rules is performative, consumer group says

BEUC urges Brussels to impose tougher penalties over alleged barriers to switching services and controlling personal data

Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

BEUC said: "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products."

The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

"Microsoft also regularly prompts users who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC said.

Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store users to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data.

Apple announced new terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC said it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance issues."

Google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA."

An Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

“A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”

BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules."

The report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®

#9984. Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

You have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every new checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

The first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

When the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

Strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

Each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise plans billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

How much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a new file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

To train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

Nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

If you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:

Buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:

A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise plans, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions announced as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

Nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

If your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

The full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

Run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's plan before anything moves.

Training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

The loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:

Stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an issue with what worked and what didn't.

Results of a internal benchmark on HF Storage Buckets

Explore the robot data lifecycle with an interactive visual guide

What makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. I came across Mobisoft Infotech while exploring this space: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

¡Qué buena onda! Esta integración de Strands Robots con los Storage Buckets de Hugging Face está perrísima para automatizar todo el flujo de trabajo en robótica sin perder tiempo ni dinero. La verdad, la deduplicación de datos a nivel de bytes con Xet y el poder entrenar modelos mediante streaming directo desde la nube nos aligera un buen el trabajo con las GPU. ¡Es una chulada total para acelerar la recolección de demostraciones y el despliegue en hardware real sin complicarse la vida! https://starzbet.mx/

#9983. Support tech fixed malware by charging client less for their services

‘I gave up at least $6,000 and I’d do it again’

Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.

"I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends."

The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.

Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.

"I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.

"He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'."

Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!

"It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product."

So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.

Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

"I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!"

Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®

#9982. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9981. GhostScript CVE 2026-125396: "Upload2Shell"

Paulos Yibelo · pwn.ai · 21 November 2026

Our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies showed how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter. In this article, we show how we reached Ghostscript through most of the applications we tested, exploited a memory corruption bug in its font loader, and bypassed its -dSAFER sandbox to achieve remote command execution across widely used software.

On 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached. The list came from following file-processing dependencies across products that otherwise had little in common.

That gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent? We continued into Ghostscript's internals and found several independent bugs of varying impact. We reported them to Artifex and worked with affected platforms to harden their file processing. Some of those bugs are still being fixed.

This article follows one of the more interesting findings. Upload2Shell, now CVE-2026-125396, is a use-after-free in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader. It gave us a write-what-where primitive: the ability to choose both the data written and its destination in native memory. A crafted document could use that control to alter the state enforcing -dSAFER and run commands as the rendering process.

Almost every application we tested with file uploads could be tricked into passing a file with a trusted extension to Ghostscript. A feature as routine as cropping an image or generating a preview could expose the interpreter. With the primitive working, we followed those conversion paths back out to their remote entry points.

Consider a PHP application generating a preview. Its code calls Imagick, the PHP binding to ImageMagick. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which may delegate the rendering to Ghostscript or another interpreter. The upload endpoint does not have to start gs itself; it only has to pass the file to a library that will.

Our WordPress-shaped preview proof reached that delegate through Imagick::readImage($input . '[0]'). The filename ended in .pdf, but the bytes were PostScript; ImageMagick handed them to Ghostscript under -dSAFER. The exploit also needed a Type 1 font file. In this delegate, it wrote the font to the scratch output path already authorized in currentpagedevice /OutputFile; another self-contained variant used Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device. Neither needed a pre-existing font file on the server.

Ghostscript can also be linked into an image-processing build as a library. In that arrangement, the interpreter runs inside the existing process instead of appearing as a separate gs command. Looking only for explicit Ghostscript calls in application code misses both kinds of indirect invocation.

An application does not need to call gs itself. In our separate decoder tests, the following ordinary image calls reached Ghostscript when given EPS content, even when the file was named .png.

Image.open() alone only identified the file in our test. Loading pixels, cropping, or converting them started the renderer.

Our source audit also found image decoding calls in InvokeAI uploads, AUTOMATIC1111 img2img, and ComfyUI previews.

We tested the calls developers use after accepting an image. Across two controlled runs on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ghostscript installed, one matrix traced 145 benign calls across 29 image APIs and the other covered additional wrappers including Imagick and imageio. We also gave the PostScript sample a .png name. It was not a valid PNG; this tested whether the decoder trusted the name or inspected the bytes. The versions below describe the tested libraries, not every product that uses them.

The decoder matters. PHP GD, OpenCV, prebuilt Sharp, Jimp, Java ImageIO, and Go's standard image decoders did not start Ghostscript for these inputs. Copying or storing a file did not render it either; the later preview or conversion is the step to inspect.

Ghostscript renders both PDF and PostScript. PostScript is a Turing-complete programming language used to describe pages, so rendering a PostScript document means executing a program. Ghostscript's -dSAFER sandbox restricts that program's file access and command execution. Like seccomp, it limits what untrusted code can do, but the enforcement is different: -dSAFER relies on checks inside the interpreter rather than a kernel-enforced system-call filter.

That still leaves a large interpreter exposed to attacker-controlled programs. As with a JavaScript engine such as V8, running the language is expected; a memory-safety bug can let a program corrupt the engine running it. An attacker can develop and test that program as a PostScript file, then deliver it through an ordinary upload.

Those permission checks matter because the rendering process has access of its own. Its service account may be able to read application files, write to disk, and start other programs. The sandbox is supposed to keep an untrusted document from using that authority. Loading a font is one of the ordinary rendering operations that must respect this boundary.

GPT 5.6 Sol, working with @PaulosYibelo, found the issue in .putgstringcopy, a helper in Resource/Init/gs_fonts.ps. Ghostscript implements parts of its own font loading in PostScript. This helper needed to write into protected font dictionaries, so it used an internal operation called .forceput.

Ordinary document code should not have that ability. The helper was bound and marked executeonly, protecting its implementation from direct inspection. But it still had to execute, and one of the operations before its privileged write could fail. The relevant sequence was:

The first line copies a string. The second performs the protected store and restores the allocation mode. The helper did not first check that its operands were of the expected types.

We registered a Type 1 font in Fontmap and loaded it with findfont. The font defined an ordinary Courier-derived face, but its loading code could see the font loader's operand stack. It replaced the filename string on that stack with a local array. In the global-to-local conversion branch, length and string allocation succeeded; copy then raised typecheck because its source was an array.

The document's error handler returned with the stack prepared for the next operation in the already-bound helper. This is the operative excerpt from our proof:

The five pops discard the failing copy, its new destination string, our substituted filename, the loader's /PathLoad key, and the loaded font dictionary. They leave the saved allocation-mode boolean on the stack. Our chosen dictionary, key, and value follow it. Execution resumes at .forceput; the subsequent setglobal consumes the boolean. We never had to call the hidden operator directly.

One implementation detail made that recovered write more than a protected-dictionary edit. In psi/zgeneric.c, .forceput temporarily treats systemdict as local while it stores the value, then restores the dictionary's space flags. A local object can therefore pass the store check into a dictionary that survives a later restore.

A protected dictionary write alone does not explain native code execution. The next step broke a separate rule: a reference must not remain usable after its object has been reclaimed.

PostScript distinguishes local and global virtual memory. Here, “virtual memory” refers to the interpreter's object spaces. A save records local memory state; a later restore discards objects created since that save. Global objects can survive that restoration.

That creates a lifetime constraint. A surviving global dictionary must not keep a usable reference to a local object that restore will free. Otherwise, restoring the local space leaves the dictionary pointing into reclaimed storage.

Our recovered store let us create precisely that relationship:

The reference in the dictionary had not changed. What occupied the address had.

A small probe made the reuse visible before we touched native memory. This excerpt omits the font setup and error handler; findfont triggers the recovered .forceput, which places a local array in systemdict:

The last read comes from Replacement; the write goes through the stale systemdict reference. If the freed allocation is reused, Replacement[1] reads 5151. The two references have reached the same bytes.

The native proof uses the same idea with a dangling 2,048-byte string and fresh arrays of integers. Each integer is 0x12345678. We scan the stale string for the marker's bytes, change its low byte from 0x78 to 0x79, then find the live array element that became 0x12345679. That identifies the overlapping slot; no absolute heap address has to be guessed.

On our 64-bit build, a Ghostscript ref occupies 16 bytes: eight bytes for its type, attributes, and size, followed by eight bytes for its value or pointer. We saved a valid integer ref for cleanup and the header of a valid writable string ref as a template. Then we placed currentdevice in the overlapping array slot, read its genuine device-reference pointer through the dangling string, and changed the live ref into a temporary string view over that pointer. The byte view let us follow Ghostscript's own pointers:

Those structure offsets describe the tested x86-64 build; the address of each object came from a live interpreter reference. This is why the proof did not depend on a fixed process address. We restored the forged ref to its original integer form before exercising file or command access.

We demonstrated native control in production image and document pipelines with a reversible change to an arithmetic operator. We copied the 16-byte mul reference, obtained a genuine sub reference, and replaced only the eight pointer bytes at offset 8 in the live mul ref. We invoked that same ref once and copied the original 16 bytes back. This was a C function-pointer change, not a PostScript definition of a new mul.

The returned page recorded the before, during, and after values:

The middle result is 29 - 11. The captured proof output also recorded NATIVE_POINTER_OVERWRITE_MATCHED=true and NATIVE_DISPATCH_RESTORED=true. For most reports, we used a simpler proof that read /proc/version and returned its contents. The arithmetic test demonstrated native control; the file read demonstrated that we had crossed Ghostscript's file-access boundary.

The same byte view gave us a target for command execution: Ghostscript's native path-control state. After walking the pointer chain above, Target was the forged string view over gs_lib_ctx_core_t. The decisive write in the proof was four PostScript put operations on native bytes:

Those bytes were path_control_active. The proof read 1,0,0,0 before the write and 0,0,0,0 after it, then confirmed that .currentpathcontrolstate was false. -dSAFER was still on the Ghostscript command line; its native file-path check had been disabled in memory.

That was not the only check. The proof first used the recovered .forceput to set the PostScript-side PermitFileWriting list to [ (*) ]. For %pipe%, parse_file_name() also consulted a cached LockFilePermissions flag. We loaded the font a third time, force-wrote that protected user parameter to false, and used save/restore to synchronize the cached value. The recorded sequence makes the separate gates visible:

The bounded Debian print job ended with this command proof, writing only a marker in /var/tmp:

The scheduler recorded PIPE_RCE_STOPPED=false, and the marker file appeared on the print server. false here means the stopped block completed. The command ran as uid=7(lp), the renderer's account, not as the person who submitted the job.

With the interpreter primitive established, the next question was where a remote user could supply the document. We traced how popular applications invoked image and PDF processing. Three cases show how different the entry points could be.

An attacker only had to send a crafted email to someone using the Roundcube server and have the recipient view the message. The sender needed no Roundcube account. The recipient did not have to click or download the attachment: displaying the email triggered the server-side processing that ran our command.

Our attachment was declared as image/jpeg and named quarterly-results.jpg, but its contents were PostScript. Roundcube treated it as an image and automatically requested a thumbnail. The thumbnail path passed the attachment to ImageMagick, which invoked Ghostscript. The document ran our proof command as www-data and produced a thumbnail.

We reached the same Ghostscript interpreter while WordPress generated a preview for an uploaded PDF. In WordPress Core, media upload privileges were enough: Authors and higher roles have them by default. Plugins using WordPress's upload and preview functions exposed the same path. WordPress's CVE-2026-65640 advisory describes remote code execution on sites using Imagick and Ghostscript. On our Linux systems, that was the stack handling the uploads.

Plugins exposed that processing to visitors without an account. In Forminator, we used a public PDF field configured to store the upload in the Media Library. That caused WordPress to generate attachment metadata and enter the Imagick conversion path. Essential Addons for Elementor's public registration widget provided another route through its upload field. Both chains ran the command as the web-service user. Once the file reached the renderer, the font-loader flaw was the same.

We also reached Ghostscript through CUPS on Debian 13 and other Linux distributions. On Debian 13, we sent an IPP Print-Job to a shared network queue that accepted jobs without authentication. CUPS passed our PostScript document to gstopdf, which started the distribution's Ghostscript with -dSAFER. The command ran on the print server as uid=7(lp).

Our RCE proof executed one fixed command and wrote a marker under /var/tmp. Requiring authentication on the queue blocked the unauthenticated submission. Shared queues that accept network print jobs without credentials expose the renderer to anyone who can reach them.

The Ghostscript CVE scores the interpreter flaw at 8.5 under CVSS 4.0. That rating uses a local attack vector. Our demonstrations reached the interpreter remotely, through both production services and the applications described here. CUPS supplied a network-exploitable print path; Roundcube supplied an email-based remote exploit; WordPress and its plugins supplied remotely exploitable upload paths. The recorded trials show that these chains were repeatable. The attacker could deliver the exploit remotely, despite the interpreter's local attack-vector classification.

The first ten rows show Upload2Shell proofs in products or their shipped components. The rows after them trace more upload and preview paths. Each entry gives the access, tested stack or pinned source revision, and the processing step that matters.

Our Ghostscript research also reached Google, Dropbox, and other production services whose names are redacted. The table brings those production services together; the Dropbox and redacted findings have separate roots from the Type 1 bug described in this article.

The renderer's account and the surrounding system controls determine what follows native memory control. That is why the table records process privileges and the observed result alongside the application name.

Here is a complete, self-contained PostScript proof of the native operator write described above. It writes its Type 1 font to Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device, triggers the font-loader flaw, reuses the freed allocation, changes a live mul reference to call sub, and restores the original bytes. No companion font file is needed.

Each step below points to its lines in the full file. The 29 × 11 check returns 319 before and after the write. While the pointer is changed, it returns 18, the result of subtraction. This proof demonstrates native memory control; the command-execution chain described above changes Ghostscript's path-control state instead.

The file changes native memory inside the rendering process. It does not execute a shell command or touch host files. On the fixed 10.08.0 build, the dangling-reference lookup failed before the pointer write.

Artifex's first fix checks the operands before .putgstringcopy can fail in copy. That closes the error path we used to recover the privileged store. A subsequent change moves the helper into C and removes its dependence on .forceput.

The first patch also explains why this kind of operation has been difficult to remove. Artifex was already working to eliminate or minimize its use. As the maintainer put it:

“it isn't easy to undo 30 years worth of assumptions in the code.” Ken Sharp, Artifex, in the fix for bug 709684

An internal font loader needed a write that ordinary document code could not perform. An error exposed that authority to the document, and the document used it to violate an object-lifetime rule. The final memory corruption depended on assumptions made at several different layers.

The applications had their own opportunities to interrupt the chain. WordPress released its Core mitigation in 7.0.4 on 12 August, with backports to older supported branches. Its application CVE and the Ghostscript CVE address different points in the processing path. For the CUPS route, queue authentication controls who can submit the document. A policy that prevents a renderer from starting a shell can limit what happens even after the interpreter is compromised.

The fix has to reach the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript inside an existing container image or application bundle. A document worker can therefore keep using vulnerable code after the host's package has been replaced.

Application hardening can close a route into the interpreter as well. The Roundcube sequence illustrates why the order of operations matters: checking a file's real type after generating its thumbnail gives the renderer the first chance to interpret it. For each downstream service, the useful question is what changed in the path from the submitted file to the rendering process.

Artifex released the root fix in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on 8 September 2026. Many distributions have since shipped it, either in that release or as a backport to an older version. Ubuntu published fixes for seven releases; Debian patched Trixie and its development branches.

The coverage is uneven. As of 12 November, Debian still listed Bookworm as vulnerable, Amazon Linux listed a pending fix, and several SUSE branches remained affected or in progress. Applications on those branches can still expose the flaw when their file-processing path reaches the affected Ghostscript package. A distribution name or a recent update to another Ghostscript CVE is not enough to establish that this bug is fixed.

The tables below record the package status for this specific flaw. Older version numbers can include a backported fix; a published fixed version does not establish that every application or container has adopted it.

As of 12 November 2026, the following vendor trackers still listed a vulnerable, affected, or pending Ghostscript package for this exact flaw. These labels describe package status, not a tested remote application path. Check the package actually installed or bundled by each service.

We did not establish whether current RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages contain the .putgstringcopy fix.

Ubuntu's USN-8949-1, published on 21 October 2026, describes our font-operand finding and lists fixed Ghostscript packages for seven releases. The notice predates the CVE assignment, so it labels this finding “No CVE number.” These are package fixes, not additional remote application tests.

Debian's tracker records the first fixed source version for Trixie and unstable. The testing branch later received the upstream-fixed package. Debian 12 remains listed vulnerable in the vendor-status table above.

The records below show packages containing upstream Ghostscript 10.08.0 or an advisory-listed fixed build. A package appearing here does not establish the first fixed date for every architecture or branch.

Fixed Ghostscript builds also reached Windows and macOS packaging channels. The availability of a package does not tell us which Ghostscript binary a particular application uses.

The dependency problem is easy to miss from the top of an application. Several layers below, a file may enter PostScript or another interpreter that never appeared in the application's security review. A review that checks only whether the upload handler accepts trusted file types can miss a vulnerability in the code that eventually processes them. A penetration test that stops at the same boundary has the same blind spot.

Alongside this Type 1 issue, our broader Ghostscript audit reached production services at Dropbox and other redacted vendors through separate findings. Each program paid its maximum bounty. Their case studies will explain the individual root causes and proofs once we have permission to publish the technical details. The series is organized around the underlying bugs as well as the products.

WordPress released its mitigation on 12 August. Artifex authored the Ghostscript fix on 2 September, committed it on 7 September, and released 10.08.0 on 8 September. We completed the Debian network CUPS proof on 17 September. The Ghostscript CVE was published on 9 November in US Eastern time.

The Debian 13 CUPS chain will be the first full case study and PoC in this series. The other product writeups will follow, with the build, delivery path, exploit result, and vendor response for each. We will add their links to the tables as they appear.

We expect other researchers to find more applications affected by this flaw. The useful place to look is the processing that follows an accepted file: thumbnail generation, metadata extraction, document import, and print conversion. Each can hand an attacker-controlled document to a process with access the sender does not have. Upload2Shell let the document use that access for itself.
