#9965. AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC

Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route

Global consultancy PwC says IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.

The Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration.

Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade.

Thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent said building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging.

Speaking to The Register, Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that.

"Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case."

SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw. With both of these new technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems.

"It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said.

An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base.

Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street, building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google.

AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®

#9964. Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:

For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:

Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-DSpark: Up to 3.2x Faster Inference from H100 to MacBook", Liquid AI Blog, Aug 2026.

#9963. Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

The attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent."

The security firm said this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec said, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

During the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he says. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering."

Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."
